task_4.title: Clarify template rendering errors outside application context
task_4.description: The 2.1.3 update improves Flask's template rendering helpers so they report a clear runtime error when used without an active application context, instead of failing with an uninformative None-related exception. Rendering behavior with a valid application context remains unchanged.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that calling Flask template rendering helpers outside an active application context produces a clear, user-facing failure that explains the context requirement instead of an ambiguous None-related error.

expectation.grounded: When `render_template` or `render_template_string` is invoked and no Flask application context is active, the call should raise `RuntimeError` immediately with an application-context-specific explanation. When an application context is active, both APIs should continue rendering templates normally using the current app and template context.
expectation.conceptual: Template rendering APIs should clearly tell developers when they are being used in the wrong context. If rendering is attempted without an active application, the failure should explicitly identify that requirement; otherwise rendering should behave as before.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the successful behavior of `render_template` or `render_template_string` when an application context exists. The only intended runtime change is the error type and clarity of the failure path when no application context is available.
constraints.conceptual: Keep normal template rendering behavior intact while improving only the invalid-context experience. The update should make failures easier to understand without introducing new requirements for valid calls.

behavior: `render_template` now detects the absence of an active application context before attempting to access the current app.
`render_template_string` now detects the absence of an active application context before attempting to access the current app.
If no application context is active, either API raises `RuntimeError` rather than surfacing an indirect None-related failure.
If an application context is active, template context updates and rendering continue with the current application as before.
acceptance_criteria: When `render_template` is called without an active Flask application context, it should fail with `RuntimeError` that clearly indicates an application context is required.
When `render_template_string` is called without an active Flask application context, it should fail with `RuntimeError` that clearly indicates an application context is required.
When either template rendering API is called with an active application context, it should continue to render successfully with the current app's template environment and context handling.
When invalid-context rendering fails, the observed failure should be direct and explanatory rather than an ambiguous error caused by dereferencing a missing current app.

task_3.title: Correct Flask instance_path selection for namespace packages
task_3.description: Flask 2.1.3 fixes automatic instance path discovery for namespace packages that are spread across multiple locations. Applications now use the instance directory associated with the namespace location that actually contains the imported app, avoiding incorrect instance folder selection when multiple projects contribute to the same namespace.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask applications using automatic `instance_path` discovery resolve the instance directory from the namespace package location that actually contains the imported application, even when the namespace spans multiple filesystem locations.

expectation.grounded: When a `Flask` application relies on automatic instance path discovery, `Flask.auto_find_instance_path()` and `find_package(import_name)` should resolve namespace-package apps from the namespace search location that contains the imported submodule or package named by the app's import name. As a result, `app.instance_path` should point to the `instance` directory adjacent to that contributing project. Resolution behavior for regular packages and plain modules should remain consistent with existing package and module origin handling.
expectation.conceptual: Automatic instance folder discovery should choose the instance directory belonging to the project that actually provides the imported Flask app, including namespace-package setups split across multiple locations.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress automatic instance path resolution for standard packages, normal modules, or single-location namespace packages. A resolved package path should only be classified as installed under the active Python prefix when it is actually located beneath that prefix.
constraints.conceptual: Existing instance-path behavior for ordinary package and module layouts should remain stable, and install-root detection should only treat packages as installed when they are truly inside the Python installation.

behavior: `Flask.instance_path` for apps imported from namespace packages is derived from the namespace location that contains the imported app, rather than from the first available namespace search path.
When the imported namespace subpackage provides its own search locations, Flask uses that subpackage's containing project to determine the instance directory.
If Flask cannot determine a more specific namespace location for the imported app, namespace-package resolution falls back to the first available namespace search path.
Regular packages and ordinary modules continue to resolve their package paths from their normal package or module origins.
Installed-package detection only treats a resolved package path as part of the Python installation when the path is actually contained within the active Python prefix.
acceptance_criteria: When a Flask app is imported from a namespace package that is contributed by multiple projects, it should set `instance_path` to the `instance` directory for the project that contains that imported app.
When another location contributes to the same namespace package but does not contain the imported app, it should not determine the selected `instance_path`.
When a Flask app is imported from a regular package or a plain module, automatic instance-path discovery should continue to resolve the instance directory as before.
When a resolved package path is not actually inside the active Python prefix, it should not be treated as installed under that prefix solely because its string form looks similar.

task_2.title: Relax Flask typing for callbacks, routes, and error handlers
task_2.description: Flask 2.1.3 updates public typing definitions so valid response hooks, route registrations, class-based views, and error-handler decorators type-check more accurately. The change is aimed at developer tooling and removes false-positive type errors without changing request handling behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.1.3 removes false-positive type-checking failures for valid Flask response hooks, route decorators, view registrations, and error handlers, while preserving existing runtime behavior.

expectation.grounded: The typing for `Flask.after_request`, `Blueprint.after_app_request`, and `after_this_request` should accept callbacks parameterized with any `werkzeug.wrappers.Response` subclass, so a callback annotated with `flask.Response` or another concrete response subclass is valid and returns the same subclass type. The decorators exposed by `route`, `get`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, `patch`, `errorhandler`, and `app_errorhandler` should preserve the decorated callable's type instead of degrading it to a generic callable. `Flask.add_url_rule` and `Blueprint.add_url_rule` should accept view callables returning `ResponseReturnValue`, where typed return forms include a direct response value, `(response_value, headers)`, `(response_value, int)`, `(response_value, int, headers)`, or a WSGI application, and header containers may be general mappings or sequences of `(name, value)` pairs.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should make Flask's public typing behave like its runtime behavior: valid response callbacks, registered views, and error handlers should be accepted by static type checkers, and decorators should keep the original callable types intact for downstream type inference.

constraints.grounded: This is a typing-only compatibility update. It must not change how requests are dispatched, how hooks and error handlers run, how responses are coerced at runtime, or what return shapes Flask accepts in practice. Existing valid application, blueprint, and class-based view code that already runs correctly should continue to run the same way after the upgrade.
constraints.conceptual: Do not introduce any runtime behavior change. The upgrade should only reduce incorrect typing friction and preserve compatibility for existing valid Flask usage.

behavior: Registering an `after_request`-style callback annotated with `flask.Response` no longer triggers a type incompatibility solely because the callback parameter is a concrete response subclass.
The response type accepted and returned by an `after_request`-style callback is preserved as the same response subclass for typing purposes.

Applying `@app.route`, `@app.get`, `@app.post`, `@app.put`, `@app.delete`, or `@app.patch` preserves the decorated view function's callable type instead of collapsing it to an untyped generic callable.
Applying `@app.errorhandler(...)` or blueprint-wide error-handler decorators preserves the decorated handler's callable type for typing purposes.
Registering views through `add_url_rule` type-checks against Flask's supported response return shapes, including tuple forms with integer status codes and mapping- or sequence-based headers.
acceptance_criteria: When an application registers an `after_request` callback typed as taking and returning `flask.Response`, it should be accepted by static type checking as a valid callback.

When a blueprint registers an application-wide after-request callback with a concrete response subclass annotation, it should be accepted without requiring the callback to be rewritten against a broader base response type.
When a view function is decorated with Flask's route shortcut decorators, the decorated object should retain its original callable typing so it can still be referenced as the same view callable type.
When `app.add_url_rule` or `blueprint.add_url_rule` is given a function or class-based view that returns supported Flask response forms, the registration should type-check successfully.
When an error handler is decorated with `errorhandler` or the blueprint-wide equivalent, the decorated handler should remain typed as that handler rather than being widened to a generic callable.

task_1.title: Lazy-load optional Flask CLI dependencies
task_1.description: Flask 2.1.3 defers importing optional CLI-only dependencies until the related CLI feature is actually used. This prevents unrelated CLI usage and module imports from depending on python-dotenv, SSL support, or entry-point metadata backports, while preserving the existing warning, validation, and plugin-loading behavior when those features are invoked.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask CLI only requires optional support modules when the corresponding CLI capability is used, so importing or running unrelated CLI functionality does not fail or take on unnecessary dependency requirements.

expectation.grounded: The `flask.cli` module should not eagerly import `dotenv`, `ssl`, or entry-point metadata support. `load_dotenv` should resolve `dotenv` only when environment file loading is requested, `FlaskGroup` should resolve metadata support only when loading commands from the `flask.commands` entry-point group, and certificate-related CLI validation should resolve `ssl` only while handling `--cert` or SSL context values. If an optional dependency is unavailable, only the affected feature should surface its existing warning or `click.BadParameter` outcome.
expectation.conceptual: The Flask CLI should lazily activate optional integrations. Missing optional libraries must not break import or unrelated commands; only the features that actually use environment-file loading, TLS certificate handling, or plugin discovery should depend on those libraries, and those features should still fail or warn appropriately when support is unavailable.

constraints.grounded: Retain the current behavior of environment-file loading when `dotenv` is installed, keep discovery of plugin commands through the `flask.commands` entry-point group, continue rejecting certificate usage with `click.BadParameter` when SSL support is unavailable, and continue recognizing `ssl.SSLContext` certificate values when SSL support exists.
constraints.conceptual: Do not change supported CLI behavior beyond narrowing when optional dependencies are loaded. Existing plugin loading, environment-file handling, and certificate validation semantics should remain consistent for users who have the relevant support available.

behavior: Importing `flask.cli` or using CLI flows that do not touch environment-file loading, certificate handling, or plugin discovery no longer requires eager imports of optional modules.

`load_dotenv` now checks for `dotenv` only when environment-file loading is invoked, so missing dotenv support affects only that feature and still results in the existing warning path when env files are requested or present.
Plugin command discovery through `FlaskGroup` resolves entry-point metadata support only when plugin commands are loaded.
Certificate option validation resolves `ssl` only during certificate-related CLI processing, and using `--cert` without SSL support still fails with `click.BadParameter`.
Key validation only treats the certificate value as an `ssl.SSLContext` when SSL support is available; otherwise it behaves as a non-context certificate input.
acceptance_criteria: When optional CLI dependencies are absent, importing Flask CLI or running commands that do not use env-file loading, certificate options, or plugin discovery should still work.

When environment-file loading is invoked without dotenv support and a target env file or default env files are present, Flask should warn that those files will not be loaded instead of failing during CLI import.
When plugin commands are requested, Flask should still discover commands registered under the `flask.commands` entry-point group.
When a user supplies `--cert` on a Python build without SSL support, Flask should reject that certificate usage with `click.BadParameter`.
When SSL support exists and the certificate value is an `ssl.SSLContext`, certificate/key validation should continue to recognize that case correctly.
